0.1 Introduction
Welcome to the online materials for the workshop “Bridging Stratigraphic Paleobiology and Phylogenetics”. This page collects all contents (code, text, references, and notes) used during the workshop.

title: Bridging Stratigraphic Palaeobiology and Phylogenetics
text:
0.2 Installation instructions
Software for phylogenetic inference is spread over multiple software systems. We will use:

git and GitHub to exchange code and collaborate on its annotation
Julia for stratigraphic forward simulations
R for phylogenetic simulations and to build models of stratigraphic paleobiology
revbayes or BEAST for phylogenetic inference
FigTree and Tracer for the visualization of posteriors
An IDE (integrated development environment) of your choice (e.g., VSCode or RStudio) to conveniently interact with this software.


0.2.1 Git and GitHub - optional


Why yet another tool, my nerds?

Git is a tool for version control, primarily for code but it works for any text-based files. For us, the most important use is that it will give us a “track-change” mode and we will be able to share everyone’s contributions with all participants live. This workshop’s purpose is not teaching git, so if you want to keep your mental resources for the science, you will be able to work through the week without using it. However, the goal we want to promote is better reproducibility of phylo/strat projects and better interaction between users and developers. For these goals, using git is essential and we want to support our community memebers in adopting it. So if you haven’t had experience with git before and you feel unsure about using it, please reach out to one of the organizers or git heros we will mark among the participants and we’ll give you a run down.


0.2.1.1 Installation

0.2.1.1.1 Get a GitHub account
Please follow the instructions on GitHub’s own Getting started page. Choose a free plan. Please note that you will need to verify your email address as one of the steps. Secondly, you will be given several options for two-factor authentication (2FA): each of them should work; choose the one that is the most familiar (the lear unfamiliar) to you. You can install the GitHub mobile app on your phone, but it is not indispensable.


0.2.1.1.2 Install a git client
There exist multiple git clients and we won’t be experienced in using all of them ourselves. The essentials are:

GitHub Desktop - a graphic user interface available for Windows and Mac, recommended for first-time users
git - a command line interface typically shipped with any Linux, can be installed on MacOS and PowerShell - recommended if you are otherwise accustomed to using the CLI

Configuration instructions will depend on which one you choose, but we focus here on first-time users, so assuming you use GitHub Desktop, you will need to sign into your GitHub account to be able to contribute.


0.2.1.1.3 Using git to collaborate
If you want to contribute code or text directly from your computer to the workshop’s open book, you will need to use operations such as switching between branches, pulling other people’s contributions, commiting your changes, and pushing your changes. You can collaborate with someone and do this together, or take a look at the instructions online and try on your own.






Tip



Remmeber: as long as you work on a separate branch, you can’t break anything - don’t hesitate to experiment, this is how you learn.






0.2.2 Julia
To install Julia, please go to the Julia Language Downloads page. It will automatically detect your system and provide a link to the correct installation file. It will install juliaup, which is a tool for managing Julia installations on your system and takes care of any version issues.


0.2.3 Installing R, R Studio, and packages
R can be directly installed from CRAN (the comprehensive R archive network) here. Choose the latest version for your operating system and follow the installation instructions. At the time of the workshop, the latest version is R 4.6.1 (“Happy Hop”).
You can interact with R using the IDE of your choice. Most R users are familiar with RStudio, which provides a lot of convenient functionality. R Studio can be downloaded from Posit here.
Once you have downloaded R, install all required packages by running the following code in R (e.g., in your R Studio console):

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("fossilsim/morphsim")
remotes::install_github("fossilsim/FossilSim")
remotes::install_github("MindTheGap-ERC/admtools")
remotes::install_github("MindTheGap-ERC/StratPal")
install.packages("TreeSim")

section: 3.2 2. Building a platform with a gappy stratigraphic record
text:
3.2 2. Building a platform with a gappy stratigraphic record

3.2.1 Facies
We use three benthic carbonate-producing facies, from fast-growing and shallow-tolerant (“euphotic”) to slow-growing and shade-tolerant (“aphotic”), each with its own maximum growth rate, light-extinction coefficient, and transport coefficient (how easily its sediment is moved downslope once produced):

facies = [
    ALCAP.Facies(
        viability_range=(4, 10),
        activation_range=(6, 10),
        production=BenthicProduction(
            maximum_growth_rate=500u"m/Myr",
            extinction_coefficient=0.8u"m^-1",
            saturation_intensity=60u"W/m^2"),
        transport_coefficient=50.0u"m/yr"),
    ALCAP.Facies(
        viability_range=(4, 10),
        activation_range=(6, 10),
        production=BenthicProduction(
            maximum_growth_rate=400u"m/Myr",
            extinction_coefficient=0.1u"m^-1",
            saturation_intensity=60u"W/m^2"),
        transport_coefficient=25.0u"m/yr"),
    ALCAP.Facies(
        viability_range=(4, 10),
        activation_range=(6, 10),
        production=BenthicProduction(
            maximum_growth_rate=100u"m/Myr",
            extinction_coefficient=0.005u"m^-1",
            saturation_intensity=60u"W/m^2"),
        transport_coefficient=12.5u"m/yr")
]

3-element Vector{CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies}:
 CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies(nothing, (4, 10), (6, 10), true, BenthicProduction(500.0 m Myr^-1, 0.8 m^-1, 60.0 W m^-2), nothing, 50.0 m yr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Facies##2#Facies##3"(), 0.0 m)
 CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies(nothing, (4, 10), (6, 10), true, BenthicProduction(400.0 m Myr^-1, 0.1 m^-1, 60.0 W m^-2), nothing, 25.0 m yr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Facies##2#Facies##3"(), 0.0 m)
 CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies(nothing, (4, 10), (6, 10), true, BenthicProduction(100.0 m Myr^-1, 0.005 m^-1, 60.0 W m^-2), nothing, 12.5 m yr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Facies##2#Facies##3"(), 0.0 m)




3.2.2 Geometry, timing, and the four core locations
The platform is a 100 x 50 grid of 150 m cells (15 km x 7.5 km), with a gentle ramp topography sloping away from the coast, and runs for 1 Myr in steps of 0.0002 Myr (5000 steps). Alongside the full-grid :topography output (big file!) and a 2D :profile slice, we save four single-pixel columns along that same profile (y = 25), from the shallow, proximal part of the ramp to the deep, distal slope. A single-pixel OutputSpec (an (Int, Int) slice) reflects that we often have access only to small spatial snapshots of a bigger sedimentary basin:

box = CarboKitten.Box{Coast}(grid_size=(100, 50), phys_scale=150.0u"m")
time = TimeProperties(Δt=0.0002u"Myr", steps=5000)
initial_topography = (x, y) -> -x / 300.0

locations = [
    (key = :col_proximal, label = "proximal ramp",   x = 10, y = 25),
    (key = :col_midplat,  label = "mid-platform",    x = 35, y = 25),
    (key = :col_margin,   label = "platform margin", x = 65, y = 25),
    (key = :col_slope,    label = "distal slope",    x = 90, y = 25),
]

output = Dict(
    :topography => OutputSpec(write_interval=100),
    :profile    => OutputSpec(slice=(:, 25)),
)

for loc in locations
    output[loc.key] = OutputSpec(slice=(loc.x, loc.y), write_interval=1)
end



3.2.3 An “icehouse”-type sea-level history leads to large gaps
Stratigraphic gaps form whenever relative sea level falls faster than subsidence can create new accommodation space: the platform top is exposed, carbonate production stops, and previously deposited sediment can be eroded away (disintegration_rate). To get relatively large gaps, we use a sea-level curve that oscillates with a high amplitude and short period compared to the subsidence rate, combined with a high disintegration rate:

sea_level = t -> 5.5u"m" * sin(2π * t / 0.18u"Myr")
subsidence_rate = 38.0u"m/Myr"
disintegration_rate = 80.0u"m/Myr"

Every 0.18 Myr the sea surface swings up and down by 5.5 m while the sea floor only subsides by about 38 m/Myr \(\times\) 0.18 Myr \(\approx\) 6.8 m per cycle. Each falling limb of the curve will push shallow parts of the platform above sea level, exposing them, before the next rise buries them again. That is our gap-generating machine.
Now we assemble the full input:

input = ALCAP.Input(
    box = box,
    ca_interval = 1,
    time = time,
    output = output,
    initial_topography = initial_topography,
    sea_level = sea_level,
    subsidence_rate = subsidence_rate,
    insolation = 400.0u"W/m^2",
    facies = facies,
    depositional_resolution = 0.5u"m",
    sediment_buffer_size = 50,
    disintegration_rate = disintegration_rate,
    lithification_time = 100u"yr",
)

CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Input("untagged run", Dict{Symbol, OutputSpec}(:col_slope => OutputSpec((90, 25), 1), :profile => OutputSpec((Colon(), 25), 1), :col_margin => OutputSpec((65, 25), 1), :topography => OutputSpec((Colon(), Colon()), 100), :col_proximal => OutputSpec((10, 25), 1), :col_midplat => OutputSpec((35, 25), 1)), TimeProperties(0.0 Myr, 0.0002 Myr, 5000), CarboKitten.Box{Coast}((100, 50), 150.0 m), CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies[CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies(nothing, (4, 10), (6, 10), true, BenthicProduction(500.0 m Myr^-1, 0.8 m^-1, 60.0 W m^-2), nothing, 50.0 m yr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Facies##2#Facies##3"(), 0.0 m), CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies(nothing, (4, 10), (6, 10), true, BenthicProduction(400.0 m Myr^-1, 0.1 m^-1, 60.0 W m^-2), nothing, 25.0 m yr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Facies##2#Facies##3"(), 0.0 m), CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.Facies(nothing, (4, 10), (6, 10), true, BenthicProduction(100.0 m Myr^-1, 0.005 m^-1, 60.0 W m^-2), nothing, 12.5 m yr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Facies##2#Facies##3"(), 0.0 m)], 1, 0, var"#5#6"(), var"#2#3"(), 38.0 m Myr^-1, 400.0 W m^-2, 50, 0.5 m, 0.0 m, 80.0 m Myr^-1, CarboKitten.Models.ALCAP.var"#Input##10#Input##11"(), 0.0001 Myr, Val{:forward_euler}, :adaptive, false, false, "./carbokitten.log")

3.4 4. The stratigraphic architecture of the platform
CarboKitten’s sediment_profile plots the :profile slice we saved above, colouring each parcel of sediment by its dominant facies and marking unconformities (subaerial-exposure surfaces) with dashed white lines:

using CarboKitten.Export: read_slice
using CarboKitten.Visualization: sediment_profile

header, section = read_slice(FILENAME, :profile)
sediment_profile(header, section)






Figure 3.1: Sediment profile along the platform, y = 25. Dashed white lines mark unconformities.




The white dashed lines are erosional/non-depositional surfaces that turn into the gaps we will quantify below. Notice how they cluster in the shallow, proximal part of the ramp (left) — this is the part of the platform that spends most time within reach of the oscillating sea level.

title: 3  Simulating the stratigraphic record
text:
3.5 5. Four stratigraphic columns
We now read back each of the four stratigraphic columns we saved earlier, and turn each one into a small “core log”: a vertical bar coloured by whichever facies contributed most sediment at each preserved interval. We use CarboKitten’s own stratigraphic-column algorithm (CarboKitten.Output.Abstract.stratigraphic_column), which corrects for sediment that was deposited and later disintegrated.

using CarboKitten.Export: read_column, extract_sac, extract_sc, age_depth_model

function column_bands(filename, loc)
    header, data = read_column(filename, loc.key)
    sac_df = extract_sac(header, data, loc.key)
    adm = age_depth_model(sac_df)[:, "adm_$(loc.key)"] |> in_units_of(u"m")

    sc_df = extract_sc(header, data, loc.key)
    facies_cols = ["sc_$(loc.key)_f$(f)" for f in 1:header.n_facies]
    sc = Matrix(sc_df[:, facies_cols])
    dominant = getindex.(argmax(sc, dims=2)[:, 1], 2)

    return adm, dominant
end

colors = Makie.wong_colors()
fig_logs = Figure(size=(700, 500))
axs = Axis[]
for (i, loc) in enumerate(locations)
    adm, dominant = column_bands(FILENAME, loc)
    ax = Axis(fig_logs[1, i], title=loc.label, xticksvisible=false, xticklabelsvisible=false)
    hspan!(ax, adm[1:end-1], adm[2:end]; color=colors[dominant[1:end-1]])
    push!(axs, ax)
end
axs[1].ylabel = "stratigraphic height [m]"
linkyaxes!(axs...)

Legend(fig_logs[2, 1:4],
    [PolyElement(color=colors[f]) for f in 1:3],
    ["euphotic (shallow, fast)", "oligophotic (mid depth)", "aphotic (deep, slow)"],
    orientation=:horizontal, tellwidth=false)

fig_logs






Figure 3.2: Stratigraphic columns (virtual cores) at four positions across the platform, from proximal (left) to distal (right).

title: 3  Simulating the stratigraphic record
section: 3.6 6. Age-depth models: where did the time go?
text:
3.6 6. Age-depth models: where did the time go?
The stratigraphic height each column reaches is cumulative: it only goes up when sediment is actually preserved. Plotting that cumulative height against time — the age-depth model — represents every interval of non-deposition or erosion into a flat, horizontal plateau: time passes, but the column does not grow. Long plateaus are large stratigraphic gaps.

fig_adm = Figure(size=(700, 450))
ax = Axis(fig_adm[1, 1], xlabel="time [Myr]", ylabel="stratigraphic height [m]",
          title="Age-depth models across the platform")

for loc in locations
    header, data = read_column(FILENAME, loc.key)
    t = header.axes.t |> in_units_of(u"Myr")
    sac_df = extract_sac(header, data, loc.key)
    adm = age_depth_model(sac_df)[:, "adm_$(loc.key)"] |> in_units_of(u"m")
    lines!(ax, t, adm, label=loc.label)
end

axislegend(ax, position=:rb)
fig_adm






Figure 3.3: Age-depth models for the four columns. Flat segments are stratigraphic gaps: intervals of time that left no rock behind at that location.




Compare the four curves: the proximal column (repeatedly exposed by the oscillating sea level) should show the longest flat plateaus, while columns further down the ramp - spending more time below wave base - tend to accumulate more continuously, at least until subsidence carries them out of the photic zone and production itself shuts down.

text:
3.7 7. Optional: exporting the columns for further analysis
If you want to work with these curves outside Julia (R, Python, a spreadsheet…), CarboKitten can export the sediment-accumulation curve, age-depth model, per-facies stratigraphic column, and water depth for a set of columns straight to CSV, plus a TOML file with the metadata (coordinates, subsidence rate, etc.) of each location:

using CarboKitten.Export: CSV, data_export

cols = Dict(loc.key => read_column(FILENAME, loc.key)[2] for loc in locations)
header, _ = read_column(FILENAME, first(locations).key)

spec = CSV(
    :sediment_accumulation_curve => "data/output/columns_sac.csv",
    :age_depth_model             => "data/output/columns_adm.csv",
    :stratigraphic_column        => "data/output/columns_sc.csv",
    :water_depth                 => "data/output/columns_wd.csv",
    :metadata                    => "data/output/columns_metadata.toml")

data_export(spec, header, cols)

3.8 Wrap-up

A single sea-level curve, applied uniformly across a platform, produces a spatially heterogeneous stratigraphic record: gap size and frequency depend strongly on where a section sits relative to sea level and the photic zone.
The age-depth model is the key object that translatesrock thickness into time.
Try changing sea_level, subsidence_rate, or disintegration_rate above and re-running from Section 3 onward: how do the four age-depth models respond? Can you find a parameter combination where the deepest column has the biggest gaps instead of the shallowest one?

title: 6  MorphSim Tutorial
text:
6.1 Simulating phylogenetic trees in R
Before we can simulate morphological data we need a phylogenetic tree along which to simulate our data. In R, trees can be simulated using a number of different packages, most commonly ape and TreeSim. Here we explain how to generate a birth-death time tree using TreeSim.
TreeSim (Stadler 2011) simulates trees under a constant-rate birth-death process, where new lineages are added at rate lambda (speciation) and removed at rate mu (extinction). The function we’ll use, sim.bd.taxa(), simulates a tree conditioned on reaching a fixed number of extant tips.
TreeSim provides several related functions depending on what you want to condition the simulation on:
We’ll focus on sim.bd.taxa() since it’s the simplest entry point, but it’s worth knowing the others exist if your own data calls for a different kind of tree.
For reproducibility, we set a random seed before simulating: since the birth-death process is stochastic, this ensures the tree (and everything downstream) is identical every time this document is rendered.
library(TreeSim)

Loading required package: ape


Loading required package: geiger


Warning: package 'geiger' was built under R version 4.6.1


Loading required package: phytools


Loading required package: maps

library(ape)

set.seed(12)

title: 6  MorphSim Tutorial
text:
Function
Conditions on




sim.bd.taxa()
number of tips


sim.bd.age()
tree age (time since root)


sim.bd.taxa.age()
both age and tip number


sim.rateshift.taxa()

sim.gsa.taxa()
number of tips, sampled from a larger pool of simulated trees







6.1.1 Generating the tree
We simulate a single tree with 10 tips, a speciation rate of 1 and an extinction rate of 0.5. Note that mu must be less than lambda; if extinction is too close to (or exceeds) speciation, the process may need many attempts to reach the target number of tips, and simulation will be slow or may not converge in reasonable time.

tree_list <- sim.bd.taxa(
  n        = 10,   # number of extant tips
  numbsim  = 1,    # number of trees to simulate
  lambda   = 1,    # speciation rate
  mu       = 0.5,  # extinction rate
  complete = TRUE # drop extinct/non-sampled lineages; keep only extant tips
)

tree <- tree_list[[1]]

Note that sim.bd.taxa() always returns a list of trees, with length equal to numbsim. Even when simulating a single tree, we still need to index into the list ([[1]]) to extract the phylo object itself. This trips a lot of people up the first time, so it’s worth calling out explicitly.
We set complete = TRUE so we want the whole tree, including lineages that went extinct before the present, rather than one pruned down to extant taxa only. It’s important to understand what n controls here: sim.bd.taxa() only lets you specify the number of extant tips, not the total number of tips in the tree. So with n = 10 and complete = TRUE, the simulation keeps adding and removing lineages until it reaches exactly 10 tips at the present, but every lineage that went extinct along the way is also retained in the output. That means the final tree will generally have more than 10 tips in total once extinct lineages are counted. If you instead want a tree with exactly 10 tips and no fossils at all, set complete = FALSE, which drops the extinct lineages and returns only the extant-tip tree.


6.1.2 Checking the tree
Before moving on to simulating morphology, it’s good practice to confirm the tree looks the way we expect. A few quick checks:

# total tip count, including BOTH extant and fossil lineages
# (this will be > 10, since n only controls extant tips)
Ntip(tree)

[1] 14



# this is the check that actually confirms n = 10 was enforced:
# count tips whose distance from the root equals the tree's max depth
# (i.e. tips sampled at the present)
node_depths <- node.depth.edgelength(tree)
tip_depths  <- node_depths[1:Ntip(tree)]
sum(abs(tip_depths - max(tip_depths)) < 1e-8)

[1] 10



# with complete = TRUE, the tree should generally NOT be ultrametric,
# since fossil tips end before the present
is.ultrametric(tree)

[1] FALSE



# branch lengths should all be positive and finite
summary(tree$edge.length)

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
0.007114 0.216468 0.480171 0.498485 0.649550 1.361996 



# TreeSim always produces a strictly bifurcating tree so this
# should be TRUE regardless of complete = TRUE/FALSE
is.binary(tree)

[1] TRUE




6.1.3 Visualizing the tree
A quick plot lets us see the fossil tips (branches ending before the present) alongside the extant ones:

plot(tree, cex = 0.8, no.margin = TRUE)








With a validated phylo object, extant and fossil tips both retained,we’re ready to simulate morphological character data along its branches using MorphSim.

title: 6  MorphSim Tutorial
text:
6.2 Simulating Morphological Data
Now that we have a validated tree (extant tips plus fossils, from TreeSim), we can simulate morphological character data along it using MorphSim. We’ll build up the model one assumption at a time, starting from the simplest possible case and progressively relaxing it, the same tree is used throughout, so any differences in the resulting data are purely down to the model, not the tree.

library(MorphSim)


6.2.1 The baseline: Mk
The simplest model for discrete morphological data is the Mk model (Lewis 2001), a direct extension of the Jukes-Cantor idea to morphology: k possible states per character, one shared substitution rate, and no direction favoured over any other. It’s a strong assumption. Unlike a nucleotide, state “1” in one character has no inherent relationship to state “1” in another, but it’s the natural starting point,.

morpho_mk <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1, trait.num = 15)
plotMorphoGrid(morpho_mk)








Take a look at the grid, you’ll likely spot at least one invariant column (a character that never changes across any tip). Real morphological datasets essentially never look like this, for a specific reason we’ll get to next.


6.2.2 MkV: conditioning on variability
Empirical matrices are curated by systematists, and nobody writes down a character that doesn’t vary, invariant characters simply aren’t scored in the first place. If we simulated data and then deleted invariant columns after the fact, we’d bias our branch length and rate estimates, since we’d have thrown away information about how rare change actually is. MkV builds the exclusion directly into the model, so the simulation (and the corresponding likelihood, if you’re fitting a model back to this data) correctly accounts for the fact that we conditioned on variability from the start.

morpho_mkv <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1,
                          trait.num = 15, variable = TRUE)



6.2.3 Making sure the state space is fully sampled
Even with k = 3 allowed, a finite simulation on a finite tree might just never sample one of those states, especially with a small tree, low rates, or few characters. If you’re using simulated data to test a 3-state model but only two states ever show up at the tips, you’ve unintentionally built a test case for a simpler model than you think you have. full.states forces the simulation to keep resampling until every state you specified actually appears somewhere in the matrix.

morpho_full <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1,
                           trait.num = 15, variable = TRUE, full.states = TRUE)



6.2.4 Filtering for parsimony-informative characters
A second, related issue: real matrices are mostly composed of parsimony-informative characters, at least two states, each seen in two or more taxa. A raw simulation will happily generate autapomorphies (a state found in only a single taxon) or characters that are technically variable but still uninformative for resolving relationships. Rather than hand-filtering afterwards, MorphSim lets you enforce this directly:

# tolerate autapomorphies
morpho_pars_standard <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1,
                                    trait.num = 15, variable = TRUE,
                                    parsimony = "standard")

# every state must occur in 2+ taxa = stricter
morpho_pars_strict <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1,
                                  trait.num = 15, variable = TRUE,
                                  parsimony = "strict")







Note



Both full.states and parsimony work by rejection sampling: generate, check, discard, and retry. If k is set too high, rates too low, or the tree too small, this can take a long time to converge, MorphSim caps at 1 million iterations and will tell you to relax a parameter if it can’t satisfy your constraints.




6.2.5 Among-character rate variation (ACRV)
So far every character has shared a single rate, which is biologically implausible: some traits are under tight functional or developmental constraint and barely change, while others are close to neutral and drift quickly. Among-character rate variation lets each character draw its own rate multiplier, typically from a discretized gamma distribution, the same approach used for among-site rate variation in molecular models.

morpho_acrv <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1, trait.num = 15,
                           variable = TRUE, ACRV = "gamma", alpha.gamma = 1, ACRV.ncats = 4)

plotMorphoGrid(morpho_acrv)








Same tree, same branch rates, the only thing that changed is the character-rate distribution. Does this look closer to a matrix you’d recognize from real data?


6.2.6 Custom Q-matrices: encoding your own assumptions
Everything above still assumes equal rates in every direction between states. That’s often wrong for a specific character rather than merely simplified. Meristic characters, or anything that must pass through intermediate states, shouldn’t be able to jump directly from state 0 to state 2. An ordered model encodes exactly that constraint:

ord_Q <- matrix(c(-0.5, 0.5, 0.0,
                   0.3333333, -0.6666667, 0.3333333,
                   0.0, 0.5, -0.5),
                nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

morpho_ordered <- sim.morpho(k = 3, time.tree = tree, br.rates = 0.1, trait.num = 15,
                              variable = TRUE, ACRV = "gamma", alpha.gamma = 1,
                              ACRV.ncats = 4, define.Q = ord_Q)

plot(morpho_ordered, trait = 1, box.cex = 2)

Note: no fossil data available, fossils will not be shown


Note: no fossil data available, reconstructed tree will not be shown









plot.morpho() lets you follow one character’s full transition history along the tree, a useful way to see the ordering constraint actually playing out branch by branch, rather than just inferring it from the tip states.


6.2.7 Partitioning the matrix
So far every character in a given call to sim.morpho() has shared the same number of states and the same model. Real morphological matrices are rarely that homogeneous, a matrix might include binary presence/absence characters, three-state characters describing shape variation, and four-state meristic counts, all in the same dataset. MorphSim handles this with the partition argument: you specify how many traits belong to each partition, and give k as a vector with the number of states for each partition (in the same order).

part_data <- sim.morpho(
  time.tree  = tree,
  k          = c(2, 3, 4),
  trait.num  = 20,
  partition  = c(10, 5, 5),
  br.rates   = 0.1
)

# model specification per partition
part_data$model$Specified

[1] "Mk_Part:10states:2" "Mk_Part:5states:3"  "Mk_Part:5states:4" 


Here, the first 10 traits are binary (k = 2), the next 5 have three states, and the last 5 have four states. The values in partition must sum to trait.num, or sim.morpho() will throw an error.






Note



partition only lets you vary the number of states (k) across groups of characters within a single call. If you want different partitions to use different models entirely for example, some ordered with a custom Q, others unordered with gamma rate variation you can’t do that in one call. Instead, simulate each partition separately with its own sim.morpho() call, then merge them with combine.morpho(). Both objects must share the same tree, branch lengths, and (if used) fossil object.



# partition 1: ordered characters with a custom Q matrix
partition_1 <- sim.morpho(time.tree = tree, k = 3, trait.num = 10,
                           br.rates = 0.1, define.Q = ord_Q)

# partition 2: unordered binary characters with MkV + gamma ACRV
partition_2 <- sim.morpho(time.tree = tree, k = 2, trait.num = 10,
                           br.rates = 0.1, variable = TRUE,
                           ACRV = "gamma", alpha.gamma = 1, ACRV.ncats = 4)

combined <- combine.morpho(partition_1, partition_2)

# 20 traits total, model info from both partitions preserved
length(combined$sequences$tips[[1]])

[1] 20

combined$model$Specified

[1] "Mk_Part:10states:3"       "MkgammaV_Part:10states:2"




6.2.8 Missing data as a taphonomic layer
Everything up to this point has been about the evolutionary process, how characters change along the tree. Real fossil matrices are also shaped by a second, independent process: preservation. Not every character that existed is observable in a fossil, and different anatomical regions have very different preservation potential. This is where stratigraphy and taphonomy come back into the picture: the pattern of missing data in a real matrix isn’t random noise, it’s a signal about what kind of tissue, environment, and depositional setting produced the fossil record you’re working with.
sim.missing.data() lets us impose that layer on top of a simulated matrix, replacing observed states with "?" under different missingness scenarios.
By partition: mirrors the character partitions we just built: some anatomical regions (e.g., robust skeletal elements) preserve far more reliably than others (e.g., soft tissue characters).

# hard tissue characters (partition 1): 10% missing
# soft tissue characters (partition 2): 70% missing
missing_part <- sim.missing.data(
  data = combined, method = "partition",
  seq = "tips", probability = c(0.1, 0.7)
)

Extinct taxa only: leaves extant tips fully observed and only introduces missing data in fossil taxa, reflecting the common (and very real) asymmetry that living specimens can be studied completely while fossils cannot.

missing_extinct <- sim.missing.data(
  data = combined , method = "extinct",
  seq = "tips", probability = 0.5
)

Other available method options worth knowing about: "random" (uniform missing data across the whole matrix, useful as a naive baseline), "rate" (missing data tied to a character’s ACRV rate category, useful for testing whether fast- or slow-evolving characters are preferentially lost), and "trait" / "taxa" / "trait_taxa" for targeting specific characters or specimens directly.


6.2.9 Exporting matrices, trees, and fossil ages
Once you’re happy with a simulated dataset, write.morpho() provides a single interface for exporting everything you need to move into downstream phylogenetic software (RevBayes, BEAST2, or similar): the tree, the character matrix, and fossil occurrence ages. The type argument controls what gets written, and reconstructed controls whether you export the full simulated tree/matrix or only the reconstructed version (i.e., only the sampled lineages, relevant once fossils are involved, see day 3).

# full tree
write.morpho(missing_part, file = "tree.tre", type = "tree",
             reconstructed = FALSE)

# character matrix
write.morpho(missing_part, file = "matrix.nex", type = "matrix", reconstructed = FALSE)

# fossil occurrence ages (compatible with RevBayes)
write.morpho(missing_part, file = "ages.tsv", type = "ages")

# ages with associated uncertainty
write.morpho(missing_part, file = "ages.tsv", type = "ages",
             uncertainty = 2)







ImportantWhy simulate at all?



Before starting the next section it is worth thinking about why we need simulation studies. It might seem backwards to spend a workshop generating fake data when the goal is to understand real fossil datasets. But simulation is one of the few tools we have for testing whether our inference methods actually recover what we think they recover.
With real data, we never know the true tree, the true model, or the true pattern of missing data, we’re always inferring all three at once, which makes it hard to tell whether a surprising result reflects real biology or a limitation of the method. With simulated data, we control every one of those pieces. That means we can:

Test methods against a known truth. Simulate under a model with a known Q-matrix, known rate heterogeneity, and known tree, then run inference on the result. Ff the method recovers something far from what you simulated, that tells you something important about its limits, not about the fossil record.
Separate process from artifact. When something looks unusual in a real matrix (e.g. surprisingly low homoplasy, or an odd concentration of missing data), simulation lets you ask: could this pattern arise just from preservation bias, even under a perfectly ordinary evolutionary process? If yes, that’s a caution against over-interpreting the pattern biologically.
Build intuition for what “normal” looks like. Once you’ve seen how an Mk matrix, an MkV matrix, and a partitioned matrix with realistic missing data each look and behave differently, you’re much better equipped to look at someone else’s real dataset and have an informed opinion about what its statistics are (and aren’t) telling you.

This is also exactly why we built the model up one assumption at a time today, rather than jumping straight to something maximally realistic: every mismatch between a simple model and a real dataset is potentially meaningful, but only if you know precisely which assumption you relaxed to close that gap.




6.2.10 Your turn: biology meets the fossil record
Everything in this section has been two separate layers stacked on top of each other: an evolutionary model (partitions, rates, Q-matrices) that describes how characters actually change, and a preservation model (missing data) that describes what we can actually observe of that change once fossils are involved. Real morphological matrices are the product of both and it’s easy to mistake a pattern caused by preservation for one caused by evolution, or vice versa, if you’re not thinking about them as distinct layers.
For this exercise, work in groups and design one scenario that combines both layers:
Step 1: the biology. Choose a partition structure that reflects a real hypothesis about your organism of interest. For example:

A skeletal dataset with slow-evolving, ordered meristic characters (limb segment counts) alongside fast-evolving, unordered characters (colour pattern, if it were preservable).
A dataset where one partition is under strong functional constraint (low rate, few states) and another is closer to neutral (higher rate, more states).

Build this with sim.morpho(), using partition and k (or combine.morpho() if your partitions need genuinely different models, not just different state numbers).
Step 2: the stratigraphy. Now decide why some of this data would be missing in a real fossil dataset, and choose a sim.missing.data() method that reflects that reasoning rather than picking probabilities arbitrarily. Questions to ground this in:

Which of your partitions corresponds to tissue that preserves well (bone, teeth) versus poorly (integument, soft anatomy)? → method =   "partition"
Are your fossil taxa systematically less complete than your extant taxa, independent of which characters they are? → method = "extinct"
Is there a specific, well-known taphonomic bias for your group, e.g., a particular character system that’s notoriously hard to score from compressed or fragmentary material? → method = "trait" or "trait_taxa"

Step 3: Are there some limitations to what we can simulate? Think about all the models you have seen so far, are there any process you think we are not capturing would be important for modeling morphological data from fossils? What assumptions could we include to improve our modeling of morphological data?

text:
10.1 Introduction
In this chapter we will explore some advanced topics in stratigraphic paleobiology, specifically
To slowly approach this, we use two data types: event data as introduced on the first day (e.g., fossil ages/locations and last occurrences) and the fossil objects simulated by FossilSim that are associated with a phylogenetic tree.

title: 10  Stratigraphic paleobiology and fossil occurrences
text:
How taphonomic and ecological effects shape the stratigraphic distribution of fossils
How the misidentification of age-depth relationships changes the inference of temporal dynamics.

title: 10  Stratigraphic paleobiology and fossil occurrences
text:
10.2 What we know
As before, we focus on one of the simulated age-depth models.

adm_location = "../data/output/columns_adm.csv" # adjust if you have a different output location
data_adm = read.csv(adm_location) # read age-depth model data
key = "mid"

t =  data_adm[,which(grepl("Myr",names(data_adm)))] # time step
# select height column that contains the key
h = data_adm[,which(grepl(key,names(data_adm)))]
# define age-depth model
adm = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = t,
                          h = h,
                          T_unit = "Myr",
                          L_unit = "m")
plot(adm,
     lwd_destr = 1, # line width destructive interval (hiatus)
     lwd_acc = 2, # line width accumulative interval
     col_destr = NULL,
     col_acc = "black")
admtools::T_axis_lab() # add time axis label
admtools::L_axis_lab()








Let’s simulate a tree over the time interval of observation and some fossils along the tree:

seed = 42
lambda = 2
mu = 0.3
psi = 70
set.seed(seed)
t_min = admtools::min_time(adm)
t_max = admtools::max_time(adm)
h_max = admtools::max_height(adm)
h_min = admtools::min_height(adm)

tree = TreeSim::sim.bd.age(age = t_max,
                              numbsim = 1,
                              lambda = lambda,
                              mu = mu,
                              frac = 1,
                              mrca = FALSE,
                              complete = TRUE)[[1]]
fossils = FossilSim::sim.fossils.poisson(rate = psi,
                                         tree = tree)
plot(fossils, tree)








These three components (age-depth model, the tree, and the fossil object) form our reference data.

title: 10  Stratigraphic paleobiology and fossil occurrences
text:
10.3 Ecological and taphonomic effects
Ecology and taphonomy act identically on fossil occurrences:

Niche preferences determine whether a taxon will be observed at a specific location/time: If some environmental gradient matches the preferred environment of the taxon it is more likely to be observed. The more the environmental cline deviates from the optimum, the more unlikely an observation is
Taphonomy conditions determine whether a fossil is preserved or not. Again, this is a joint expression of an environmental gradient (e.g., water depth, grain size, burial velocity) and an intrinsic property, meaning the preservation probability under the specified taphonomic conditions.

For this example, we focus on water depth as an ecological gradient for simplicity. Generally, and gradient/model output can be used.
Let’s start by importing the water depth:

wd_location = "../data/output/columns_wd.csv" # adjust if you have a different output location
data_wd = read.csv(wd_location) # read age-depth model data
key = "mid"
t =  data_wd[,names(data_wd)[2]] # time step
# select height column that contains the key
wd = data_wd[,which(grepl(key,names(data_wd)))]

plot(x = t,
     y = wd,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Water depth [m]",
     main = "Water depth")








Next we need to define a niche, which specifies how likely it is to observe a taxon at a given water depth. Here we use a helper function for this:

niche_def = StratPal::snd_niche(opt = 5, # pref. water depth 5 m
                                tol = 10, # water depth tolerance 10 m (sd)
                                cutoff_val = 0) # does not live above water 
wd_vals = seq(from = min(wd),
              to = max(wd),
              length.out = 100)
plot(x = wd_vals,
     y = niche_def(wd_vals),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Water depth [m]",
     ylab = "Sampling probability",
     main = "Niche definition")








The next piece of information is to encode the environmental gradient as a function

gradient = approxfun(x = t,
                     y = wd)
plot(x = t,
     y = gradient(t),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Water depth [m]",
     main = "Water depth as gradient")








Combining the two gives the sampling probability with time:

plot(x = t,
     y = t |> gradient() |> niche_def(),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time",
     ylab = "Sampling probability",
     main = "Sampling probability of taxon")








Note that here the sampling probability drops to 0 not because of erosion or a hiatus, but because the simulated taxon is strictly marine.

10.3.1 Effect on fossil occurrences
With these pieces of information in place - niche and gradient - we can start to simulate how ecology would influence the abundance of a taxon:

# baseline scenarion without ecological effects
StratPal::p3_var_rate(x = c(0,1),
                      y = c(1,2),
                      from = 0,
                      to = 1,
                      n = 1000) |>
  hist(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.05),
       main = "Baseline without ecological effect",
       xlab = "Time",
       ylab = "Fossil occurrences")

Warning in rej_samp(f = f, x_min = from, x_max = to, n = n, f_max = f_max):
f_max < f on between x_min and x_max. f_max was adjusted to be 2.14358881









To incorporate the ecological effects, you simply insert apply_niche into the pipeline:

StratPal::p3_var_rate(x = c(0,1),
                      y = c(1,2),
                      from = 0,
                      to = 1,
                      n = 1000) |>
  StratPal::apply_niche(niche_def = niche_def,
                        gc = gradient) |>
  hist(breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = 30),
       main = "Fossil abundance with ecological effect",
       xlab = "Time",
       ylab = "Fossil occurrences")

Warning in rej_samp(f = f, x_min = from, x_max = to, n = n, f_max = f_max):
f_max < f on between x_min and x_max. f_max was adjusted to be 2.14358881









It is then simple to insert stratigraphic effects into the pipeline to study the joint effect:

StratPal::p3_var_rate(x = c(0,1),
                      y = c(1,2),
                      from = t_min,
                      to = t_max,
                      n = 1000) |>
  StratPal::apply_niche(niche_def = niche_def,
                        gc = gradient) |>
  admtools::time_to_strat(adm) |>
  hist(breaks = seq(from = 0, to = h_max, length.out = 30),
       main = "Fossil abundance with ecological effects\nin the stratigraphic domain",
       xlab = "Stratigraphic position",
       ylab = "Fossil occurrences")

Warning in rej_samp(f = f, x_min = from, x_max = to, n = n, f_max = f_max):
f_max < f on between x_min and x_max. f_max was adjusted to be 2.14358881









That’s how easy this is!


10.3.2 Application to fossil objects associated with phylogenetic trees
Everything said above applies identical to fossil objects simulated along a tree: Define a niche (valid for all taxa record in the tree) and a gradient, and use apply_niche. There is one major caveat though: age-depth models count time forward as the simulation evolved, while fossil objects record *age. This requires flipping the time axis to make everything work out correctly:

# As baseline
plot(fossils, tree,
     main = "Full fossil record without ecological effects")








Now let’s introduce the ecological effects:

fossils_after_ecol = fossils |>
  admtools::rev_dir(ref = t_max) |>
  StratPal::apply_niche(niche_def = niche_def, gc = gradient) |>
  admtools::rev_dir(ref = t_max)
plot(fossils_after_ecol, tree)








Note the significant thinning of fossil sampling towards the top of the tree due to repeated subaerial exposure. Note again that this effect has nothing to do with gaps, just the fact that the taxon does only live underwater.


10.3.3 Taphonomic effects
Taphonomic effects are modeled identical to ecological effects, with the taphonomic gradient (e.g., burial velocity) taking the role of the ecological gradient, and the preservation potential taking the role of the niche definition.
As a simple example, we define a taphonomic gradient that filters all occurrences that fall in a gap:

# defines taphonomic filter that removes all fossils coinciding with gaps
f = StratPal::strat_filter(adm)
fossils_filtered = fossils |>
  admtools::rev_dir(ref = t_max) |>
  StratPal::apply_taphonomy(identity, f) |>
  admtools::rev_dir(ref = t_max)

plot(fossils_filtered, tree,
     main = "Fossils during gaps removed")








Of course this pipeline can be extended to include stratigraphic effects and multiple ecological and taphonomic gradients.


10.3.4 Extensions and limitations
Both ecological and taphonomic effects work out of the box for multivariate functions due the the magic of function composition. However, this modeling approach does currently not allow to model state-dependent effects (e.g., evolution of niches, variations in preservation between branches). In addition, this does not yet integrate with MorphoSim to selectively remove characters.

title: 10  Stratigraphic paleobiology and fossil occurrences
text:
10.4 Age misidentification
Up to now, we have assumed that age-depth models are fully known, which in reality is never really the case. Here we examine how this can effect interpretations of temporal dynamics.
The underlying idea is that there are 2 age-depth models at play: a “true” age-depth model that is used for forward modeling to determine the stratigraphic distribution of fossils, and a “assumed” age-depth model that is in a second step used to reconstruct ages from the observed stratigraphic positions of fossils.
Let’s assume the simulated age-depth model is our true model, and our assumed model assumes naively that sediment accumulation is constant over the observed time interval:
adm_true = adm # "truth"
adm_assumed = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = seq(t_min, t_max, length.out = 1000),
                                  h = seq(h_min, h_max, length.out = 1000),
                                  T_unit = "Myr",
                                  L_unit = "m")
plot(adm_true)
title(main = "True age-depth model")
plot(adm_assumed)
title(main = "Assumed age-depth model")











10.4.1 Effect on fossil occurrences and last occurrences
To determine the inferred age of a fossil, first determine its stratigraphic position using the correct age-depth model, and the reconstruct its age using the assumed age-depth model:

true_age = 0.75
assumed_age = true_age |>
  admtools::time_to_strat(adm_true) |>
  admtools::strat_to_time(adm_assumed)
assumed_age

[1] 0.8250585


This immediately generalizes, e.g. under a constant extinction rate (and assuming every taxon is abundantly sampled), the reconstructed pattern of last occurrences is

StratPal::p3(rate = 1,
   from = t_min,
   to = t_max,
   n = 1000) |>
  admtools::time_to_strat(adm_true, destructive = FALSE) |>
  admtools::strat_to_time(adm_assumed) |>
  hist(breaks = seq(from = t_min, to = t_max, length.out = 30),
       xlab = "Time [Myr]",
       main = "Inferred extinction dymanics",
       freq = FALSE,
       ylab = "Last occcurrences")








Think through this to validate that the peaks in the histogram correspond to the gaps in the age-depth model.
This approach allows to immediately determine how wrong our age-estimates really are due to the wrong age-depth model:

inferred_time = t |> 
  admtools::time_to_strat(adm_true) |>
  admtools::strat_to_time(adm_assumed)  
plot(x = t,
     y = t - inferred_time,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Error [Myr]")
lines(x = c(t_min, t_max),
      y = c(0,0),
      lty = 3)










10.4.2 Application to fossil objects associated with a tree
As before, this approach immediately expands to fossil objects simulated along a tree, again with the complication that the direction of time needs to be flipped:

fossils_misassigned_age = fossils |>
    admtools::rev_dir(ref = t_max) |>
  admtools::time_to_strat(adm_true) |>
  admtools::strat_to_time(adm_assumed) |>
    admtools::rev_dir(ref = t_max)
plot(fossils_misassigned_age, tree,
     main = "Tree with wrong reconstructed fossil ages")








Here you can immediately see the contradiction between the timing of the underlying biological truth (the tree) and the (wrongly) reconstructed ages of the fossils. At multiple locations, fossils associated with a lineage extend beyond the duration of the lineage, and fossils of an ancestoral lineage are present long after a branching event.
Using these fossil ages for tree inference will clearly lead to wrong results.

title: 11  Phylogeny and stratigraphy
text:
11.1 Introduction
This chapter combines everything we have learned so far by combining stratigraphic paleobiology and phylogenetics into one forward simulation. At the end of this chapter, you will have built a complete simulation pipeline consisting of
With all these pieces in place, we can then address two key questions in the next chapter:
Your task for this chapter is to modify the provided pipeline according to your work in the last 3 days and simulate your very own fossil record. At the end you should have two components: (1) simulated biased data that you would usually use for inference, specifically a character matrix and fossil ages and (2) the biological and stratigraphic “truth” to compare inference results to. Specifically, this should contain the true sampled tree, age-depth relationship, clock rate, and model of morphological evolution.

title: 11  Phylogeny and stratigraphy
text:
A stratigraphic forward model (CarboKitten) that simulates age-depth models and environmental gradients such as water depth and facies
A FBD tree that describes the evolutionary relationship between taxa
Fossils sampled along the tree according to an originally constant sampling rate, which is modified by gaps in the stratigraphic record and ecological as well as taphonomic effects
A character matrix for the fossils evolving according to a specified model of evolution and potentially missing characters due to differential preservation
Fossil ages that are potentially offset due to age misassignment or uncertain



When we run inference on the simulated data (fossil ages, character matrices), can we recover the “true” evolutionary history (e.g., tree topology, model parameters)? More speculatively, can we potentially recover stratigraphic information such as sediment accumulation rates and gap duration from phylogenetic inference?
Having build the forward simulation pipeline, can we use our knowledge of stratigraphy and the sampling process as sources of information in the inference? And if yes, does it improve the inference?

12.3 Providing stratigraphic data into phylogenetic inference
Add stratigraphic information to the inference by using the FBD skyline model. Use the skyline for the sampling rate to distinguish between intervals where (1) you know nothing can be sampled due to gaps in the fossil record, (2) intervals where fossils are sampled and you have an estimate of the sampling rate available and (3) intervals where fossils are sampled but you have no estimate of the sampling rate.

You can use the following code to determine the breakpoints of your skyline model more easily:

get_skyline_breakpoints = function(adm,
                                   min_gap_duration){
  #' determines skyline breakpoints (in age)
  #' for gaps above a minimum gap duration
  #' @param adm an age-depth model
  #' @param min_gap_duration positive number, minimum gap duration to filter by
  #' 
  #' @description
    #' does return breakpoints in age!
    #' 
  t_max = admtools::max_time(adm)
  hiat_mat =  do.call(rbind, admtools::get_hiat_list(adm))
  long_enough = (hiat_mat[, "end"] - hiat_mat[, "start"]) > min_gap_duration
  long_hiat = hiat_mat[long_enough,2:3] |> 
    t() |>
    as.vector()
  # convert to age
  breakpoints = rev(t_max - long_hiat)
  return(breakpoints)
}

Another useful helper function to construct priors is to determine the average effective sampling rate over an age interval:

avg_sampling_age = function(adm,
                            niche_def,
                            gradient,
                            gap_remove,
                            age_1,
                            age_2,
                            psi){
  #' determines average effective sampling rate
  #' @param adm age-depth model
  #' @param nich_def niche definition
  #' @param gradient ecological gradient
  #' @param gap_remove stratigraphic filter as defined in previous chapter
  #' @param age_1 first age
  #' @param age_2 second age
  #' @param psi fossil sampling parameter from the FBD model
  #' 
  #' @description
  #' determines the average effective sampling rate for the interval between
  #' age_1 and age_2
  #' 
  total_sampling_rate = function(x){
    y = psi * niche_def(gradient(x)) * gap_remove(x)
    return(y)
  }
  t_max = admtools::get_max_time(adm)
  t_1 = t_max - age_1
  t_2 = t_max - age_2
  t_lower = min(c(t_1, t_2))
  t_upper = max(c(t_1, t_2))
  integral = integrate(f = total_sampling_rate,
                       lower = t_lower,
                       upper = t_upper,
                       subdivisions = 1000)[[1]]
  avg_sampling = integral/(t_upper - t_lower)
  return(avg_sampling)
}

Note that if you have subsampled your fossils to reduce sample size, this will not match the effective sample size on the FBD tree.

13.2.1 Standard FBD inference
This as a simple setup for a constant rate FBD inference. For more complex cases (e.g., age uncertainty, total evidence etc.) see this tutorial.
We use this basic setup, available in the file fbd_inference_base.rev:

char_mat <- "char_mat.nex"
taxon_ages <- "ages.tsv"
#init_tree_name <- "INSERT_HERE" - not used, if you want to initialize the starting tree
outfile <- "trace"
treefile <- "trees"
outfile_name <- outfile + ".log"
treefile_name <- treefile + ".log"

# import data
morph <- readDiscreteCharacterData(char_mat)
taxa <- readTaxonData(taxon_ages)

# true model parameters to specify initial state & priors if needed
rho <- 1.0
true_origination_rate <- 2
true_extinction_rate <- 0.3
true_sampling_rate <- 10
true_origin_time <- 2
true_clock_rate = 0.5

# initialize moves
moves = VectorMoves()

# load tree model
source("model_fbd_const.rev")
# load clock model
source("model_clock.rev")
# load model of morphological evolution
source("model_morpho.rev")

phy_morpho ~ dnPhyloCTMC(tree = fbd_tree, branchRates = branch_rates_morpho, Q = Q_morpho, type = "Standard", coding = "all")
phy_morpho.clamp(morph)

my_model = model(phy_morpho)
#my_model.graph("fbd_base.dot") generate model graph


# initialize monitors
monitors = VectorMonitors()
# write state to tracefile
monitors.append( mnModel(filename=outfile_name, printgen=10) )
# write tree to tree file
monitors.append(mnFile(filename = treefile_name, printgen = 10, fbd_tree))
# output to the screen
monitors.append(mnScreen(printgen=100, origin_time, speciation_rate, extinction_rate) )

# initialize mcmc
mymcmc = mcmc(my_model, monitors, moves, nruns = 2, ntries = 10000)
mymcmc.burnin(generations=2000,tuningInterval=1500, verbose = TRUE)
mymcmc.operatorSummary()
mymcmc.run(generations = 10000)
mymcmc.operatorSummary()

q()

Note that the “true” model parameters are provided. This is to accelerate convergence by defining appropriate priors and set the initial state of the analysis. Empirically, this is would never be the case.
The base analysis calls the three key model components: clock, morphological model, and tree model.
The clock model is specified in model_clock.rev:

# strict morphological clock
branch_rates_morpho ~ dnExponential(lambda = 1/true_clock_rate) 
branch_rates_morpho.setValue(true_clock_rate)
moves.append( mvScale(branch_rates_morpho, weight = 5.0, lambda = 0.1))
moves.append( mvScale(branch_rates_morpho, weight = 5.0, lambda = 1.0))
moves.append( mvScale(branch_rates_morpho, weight = 5.0, lambda = 10.0))

The morphological model is specified in model_morpho.rev:

# model of morphological evolution
# Mk2 model  - no ascertaintment correction
Q_morpho := fnJC(2)

And last, the tree model is specified in model_fbd_tree.rev:

speciation_rate ~ dnExponential(lambda = 1/true_origination_rate) # set to true mean
moves.append( mvScale(speciation_rate, weight=5.0, lambda = 0.1) )
moves.append( mvScale(speciation_rate, weight=5.0, lambda = 1.0) )
moves.append( mvScale(speciation_rate, weight=5.0, lambda = 5.0) )
speciation_rate.setValue(true_origination_rate)

extinction_rate ~ dnExponential(lambda = 1/true_extinction_rate) # set to true mean
moves.append( mvScale(extinction_rate, weight=5.0, lambda = 0.1) )
moves.append( mvScale(extinction_rate, weight=5.0, lambda = 1.0) )
moves.append( mvScale(extinction_rate, weight=5.0, lambda = 5.0) )
extinction_rate.setValue(true_extinction_rate)

origin_time ~ dnExponential(lambda = 1.0)
moves.append( mvScale(origin_time, weight=5.0, lambda = 0.1) )
moves.append( mvScale(origin_time, weight=5.0, lambda = 1.0) )
moves.append( mvScale(origin_time, weight=5.0, lambda = 5.0) )
origin_time.setValue(true_origin_time)

psi ~ dnExponential(lambda = 1/true_sampling_rate)
psi.setValue(true_sampling_rate)
moves.append( mvScale( psi, weight = 5.0, lambda = 0.1) )
moves.append( mvScale( psi, weight = 5.0, lambda = 1.0) )
moves.append( mvScale( psi, weight = 5.0, lambda = 10.0) )


fbd_tree ~ dnFBDP(origin=origin_time, lambda=speciation_rate, mu=extinction_rate, psi=psi, rho=rho, taxa=taxa)

moves.append( mvFNPR(fbd_tree, weight=20.0) )
moves.append( mvGPR(fbd_tree, weight = 10.0))
moves.append( mvCollapseExpandFossilBranch(fbd_tree, origin_time, weight=50.0) )
moves.append( mvNodeTimeSlideUniform(fbd_tree, weight=10.0) )
moves.append( mvNodeTimeScale(fbd_tree, weight = 20.0))
moves.append( mvRootTimeSlideUniform(fbd_tree, origin_time, weight=50.0) )
moves.append( mvSubtreeScale(fbd_tree, weight = 10.0))
moves.append( mvTreeScale(fbd_tree, origin_time, weight = 10.0))

With all these parts in place, you can run the analysis

rb fbd_inference.rev

in your terminal. This might take a while, and there are useful tools such as nohup (for Linux) that allow you to run these analyses in the background:

nohup rb fbd_inference.rev > out.log 2>&1 &
